recent.topic: Reading the consolidation base to define a precise, auditable pivot trigger — and why the throwback to the level, not the breakout through it, is the higher-expectancy swing entry
recent.summary: The base-and-pivot framework (O'Neil's cup-with-handle, Minervini's VCP) exists to convert a fuzzy 'wait for confirmation' into ONE auditable price level: the pivot — the base's prior peak / handle high, the last ceiling of overhead supply. A valid VCP base shows 2-3 successive contractions where BOTH price range AND volume tighten, each smaller than the last, signaling sellers drying up; the classic entry then buys as price clears the pivot on volume ~40-50% above average. But the empirical record undercuts the 'chase the volume breakout' half. Bulkowski's pattern database (reported ~40,000+ trades on thepatternsite.com; I could not fetch the primary page directly and cite these figures as reported by secondary summaries) finds throwbacks occur ~50-60% of the time overall and ~74% when the breakout comes on ABOVE-average volume, and that ~97% of upward-breakout pattern TYPES perform BETTER when no throwback occurs — the strongest breakouts run away and never offer a second chance, while high-volume 'confirmed' breakouts are precisely the ones that throw back most. My own 12-year ablation says the same from the entry side: confirmed_breakout (new 20d high on >=1.5x volume) scored -0.32pp ATR-matched at 21d and ADX>25 breakouts were negative in 10 of 12 years, while the low-volume no_supply_pullback was the ONE positive read (+0.22/+0.25pp). Practitioner consensus reconciles this: buying the throwback/retest to the pivot (now acting as support) on drying volume gives a better
recent.how_to_apply: For every watchlist name, read its base and write the PIVOT — the prior peak / handle high, cross-checked against anchored_vwap — as the would_buy_at level, plus an explicit event-date gate when a catalyst window applies, which fixes the AMD compound-trigger-fired-5-days-early defect (LP-0693555695). Prefer the entry my own data rewards: the throwback to that pivot on drying, no_supply_pullback volume (KB-6241168493), with the stop just below the base low so it sits beyond the sqrt(t) noise band (KB-2388376284) and the 2:1 RR floor clears honestly because I am buying AT the level, not extended above it. Do not make the volume breakout my primary entry and do not reject a setup because its breakout was unconfirmed — confirmed_breakout scored -0.32pp and breakout volume is descriptive-only. When a genuine fat pitch is running away in a supportive tape with a catalyst forcing urgency, take a 50-70% starter on the breakout and add on the retest rather than chasing full size or missing it. Accept that some of the strongest breakouts never come back: that is the priced cost of the higher-RR retest entry, not a process failure — consistent with ~30% of my regret_misses being market-wide m

recent.topic: Kelly-fraction intuition for the 1% risk budget: why deep-fractional Kelly is correct under parameter uncertainty, and how it explains the 2:1 RR floor and the conviction tier
recent.summary: The Kelly criterion f* = W - (1-W)/R maximizes long-run geometric growth (E[log wealth]) and outputs the fraction of capital to RISK - which maps exactly onto this system's 1%-of-equity, entry-to-stop budget. Running it on my own realistic parameters (2:1 RR floor so R is about 2, swing win rates 40-55% per CLAUDE.md) gives full-Kelly risk fractions of 10% (at 40% wins), 17.5% (45%), 25% (50%), and 32.5% (55%). So the 1% budget is roughly 1/10 to 1/30 of full Kelly - deeper than even quarter-Kelly - and that is correct, not timid, for three compounding reasons the literature is unanimous on. First, parameter uncertainty: MacLean-Thorp-Ziemba showed a 10% overestimate of edge causes about 50% overbetting at full Kelly, the penalty for overbetting FAR exceeds the cost of underbetting, and Thorp always ran fractional Kelly in practice; with only 2 closed trades my true edge is essentially unknown, and Kelly with unknown edge says bet near zero. Second, the growth-rate curve is a downward parabola g(c*f*) approximately (2c - c^2)*g_max: half-Kelly captures about 75% of maximum growth at half the position size, quarter-Kelly about 44%, growth hits ZERO at 2x Kelly, and beyond 2x it goes negative into near-certain ruin - so the over side has a cliff the under side does not, making underbetting strictly the safer error. Third, Kelly assumes independent bets; correlated simultaneous positions share ONE Kelly budget (the multivariate form is f* = inverse-covariance times excess return
recent.how_to_apply: Keep sizing every BUY at the 1% risk budget and read it as intentional deep-fractional Kelly, not caution to apologize for: with 2 closed trades my edge is unmeasured, so betting small IS the mathematically correct response to unknown edge, and I should stop treating the 1% floor as a bar that makes setups feel too small to bother taking. When tempted to argue for the conviction tier (1.5%), require what Kelly requires: a genuinely higher, PROVEN edge (the validator's 15 trades + 55% win rate in the 0.70+ bucket, confidence >=0.75, zero risk-desk haircut, corroborating evidence) - never step up the fraction on a narrative, because the overbetting penalty is asymmetric and a wrong edge estimate over-allocates hard. Treat the 2:1 RR floor as non-negotiable expectancy geometry, not paperwork: below it there is no positive Kelly fraction to size, so never widen a stop or inflate a target to scrape past it. On correlated adds, remember co-moving names share one Kelly budget - the 8% heat and 2% theme-risk caps are that constraint, so size the pair as one bet (KB-1223831607) rather than two independent 1% risks. recent.topic: The options-implied expected move and earnings IV crush: reading options_signals to time swing entries around binary prints, and why the implied move is a market-priced noise band
recent.summary: Options price a stock's expected move as Price × IV × √(DTE/365) ≈ one standard deviation; a fast earnings shortcut is ~0.85 × the ATM front-month straddle (tastytrade uses a weighted straddle+strangle version). Empirically the stock stays inside that ±1σ band ~68-70% of the time, so the implied move is a genuine, horizon-scaled noise band — not a forecast of direction. Crucially it is priced too WIDE on average: implied vol exceeds realized vol by roughly 3-5 percentage points annualized (the volatility risk premium), and a CBOE study of ~10 years of S&P 500 earnings found the actual post-print move was SMALLER than the straddle-implied move in ~72% of cases. But the distribution has fat tails — the ~30% of moves that break the band include the outliers that gap through any stop (the SMCI ~20% preliminary-print pop is exactly this tail). Before a known binary event, front-month IV inflates and the term structure goes into BACKWARDATION (near-term IV > far-term); the moment the event resolves, IV crushes 30-50% (40-55% on high-IV names like NVDA/TSLA) within hours and the term structure normalizes. For a directional trader, holding a swing stop THROUGH a print means betting on a coin-flip gap you are not paid to take: the pre-print premium is a cost to option holders, but to an equity holder the print is just an un-stoppable jump on top of the normal diffusion. The cleaner trade is around it — enter 1-2 days after the print once the gap settles, IV has crushed, and the direct
recent.how_to_apply: Before any BUY, read options_signals.expected_move_pct and term_structure together with days_to_earnings: if a print (or a backwardation + high-iv_rank event premium) falls inside holding_horizon_days, default to trading AROUND it — either enter after the print once IV crushes and the gap settles, or shorten the horizon so the stop never has to survive the binary, because the earnings expected move is a discrete jump no ATR-floored stop inside the 15% cap can cover (this refines KB-2388376284: the implied move is a market-priced noise band, superior to ATR×√N, and stop_engineering already floors the stop at ½ the expected move — treat that as a one-day floor, not horizon-adequate through an event). Only hold through a print when the binary itself is the thesis (a stated drift/gap_held_revisions_up setup per KB-2596574918), and then size on gap-adjusted risk. Use term-structure backwardation and iv_rank as the detector that fired wrong on AMD — an elevated front-month event premium 5 days out means the setup is NOT live yet, so suppress the trigger until the event passes. recent.topic: Estimate-revision momentum: how upward EPS/revenue revision breadth leads price via the post-forecast-revision drift, and why breadth + price-confirmation beats a lone divergence
recent.summary: Analyst estimate revisions are a genuine, well-documented fundamental predictor: prices underreact to revisions and DRIFT in their direction for roughly six months (the post-forecast-revision drift, PFRD). Old evidence (Givoly/Lakonishok-era) put the up-minus-down revision portfolio spread near ~3% annually, and later work finds aggregated revisions can predict post-earnings-announcement returns as well as or better than the earnings surprise itself. The mechanism is the reason it persists and is the key to trading it: the DIRECTION of revisions is far more persistent than the direction of returns because analysts themselves underreact — anchoring-and-adjustment and herding make them revise incrementally and insufficiently, so a first up-revision statistically predicts more up-revisions (Chen et al. 2020, JBFA). Signal quality is not uniform. A single revision is mostly noise, and noise/bias in analyst forecasts rises with the forecast horizon (Noise in Expectations, RFS 2024), so BREADTH — how many analysts are raising vs cutting over ~100 days — and NEAR-TERM (next-quarter/next-FY) revisions carry the real signal, not one far-out number. Consistency matters more than magnitude: high-innovation revisions that are CONSISTENT with the prior trend and with price action drive more drift than larger 'reversal' revisions that fight the tape (Chen 2025), and revisions that merely drift toward existing consensus ('low-innovation') carry little information. recent.how_to_apply: Treat fundamental_screen.top_upward_revisions and revision_direction=up / positive eps_growth_next_yr_pct as a real candidate lane, not background noise — this is the direct fix for repeatedly defaulting MU-type names to the watchlist and eating +15% regret_misses. When underwriting one, weight BREADTH of near-term (30-day EPS / next-Q) revisions over any single number, and require the revision trend to be consistent (up-revisions following up-revisions), because that persistence is where the edge lives. For the fat pitch, demand price CONFIRMATION of the fundamentals — positive rel_strength_1m/3m, no_supply_pullback or a reclaim — which is precisely the post_earnings_drift_candidate gap_held_revisions_up read; that revisions-and-price-AGREE case gets full weight and can clear the bar now. recent.topic: Exit on pre-committed invalidators, not real-time conviction: the disposition effect, 'resulting', and why the written plan (not the mood) must license every early exit
recent.summary: My single binding process_fail is HPE: I closed a LOSING position ahead of its stop on a 'conviction crack,' graded process_fail with tag missing_invalidators_on_plan. The behavioral literature explains why that class of decision loses systematically. Odean's canonical study of 10,000 brokerage accounts (Journal of Finance 53:1775-1798, 1998) documents the disposition effect: investors are 1.5-2x more likely to sell a winner than a loser, and crucially this is NOT justified by subsequent returns - the losers they clung to did not go on to outperform, so the discretionary exit judgment was simply wrong on average. The practitioner consensus fix is pre-commitment: a 1991 study found the disposition effect weakens sharply when people sell at predetermined rules/intervals instead of discretionarily, and the reliable antidotes are predefined exit rules set BEFORE entry, mechanical stop/target execution, and documenting the rationale so the exit is a rule-check rather than a fresh emotional decision. Annie Duke's 'resulting' sharpens this: judging a decision by its outcome corrupts learning, so you must write the reasoning and the expected outcome distribution up front and grade the exit against THAT, not against the P&L - which is exactly why DELL (stop fired as planned, still a loss) is a process_win while HPE (discretionary, happened to save a few dollars) is a process_fail. Grade every exit against the entry plan, not the P&L (Duke's resulting): a stop firing as written is a process_win even at a loss, a discretionary save is a process_fail. recent.topic: The pullback-continuation entry in a leading uptrend: buying the low-volume ('no-supply') dip to structural support instead of chasing the fresh high
recent.summary: The pullback-continuation setup buys a temporary dip inside an established uptrend rather than chasing a new high. It works because two well-documented return patterns run on different clocks: medium-term momentum persists over roughly 3-12 months while short-term returns (days to a few weeks) mean-revert (the short-term reversal effect, Blitz/Huij, Alpha Architect summaries). Buying the short-term dip in a medium-term leader therefore rides the durable trend while getting a better price and a tighter stop. The whole craft is separating a HEALTHY pullback -- shallow, orderly, on DRYING volume, the Wyckoff/VSA 'no supply' bar where professionals simply stop selling -- from a REVERSAL, which is sharp, wide-range, and comes on HIGH volume that breaks structure ('supply'). Volume is the tell, not price alone. Minervini's version: after a valid advance a healthy pullback retraces modestly (~8-10% max, or back to a rising 50-DMA), volume contracts into the dip and re-expands on the resumption; common support zones are the 20-EMA, 50-DMA, and the 38-62% Fibonacci band. Critically, the entry is the RESUMPTION, not the dip itself -- you wait for volume to dry up and then a confirming up-move, you do not catch the falling knife. This is the one thing my own 12-year ablation confirmed: no_supply_pullback scored +0.22pp (21d) / +0.25pp (63d), the only positive read among ~25 indicators tested, measured on names already above their 200-DMA. Reported win rates vary wildly and the high ones
recent.how_to_apply: When a universe leader (above a rising 50/200-DMA, positive rel_strength_1m and 3m vs SPY) pulls back, treat it as a BUY candidate only when the dip is orderly AND volume_signal reads no_supply_pullback -- my one ablation-confirmed tell; a high-volume, wide-range dip is supply, so pass. Do not buy the dip itself: wait for volume to dry up and a resumption bar (reclaim of a short-term level or a pocket-pivot-style up day), which is the concrete fix for my ANET regret_miss where I watched the pullback and never entered. Anchor the stop just below the pullback's swing low or the named anchored_vwap level so the same stop sits beyond the noise band per KB-2388376284, hold the 2:1 RR floor honestly, and let the chandelier trail run the winner rather than tightening early. Prefer pullbacks with a catalyst inside a short window so entry-to-event noise is small, and size the initial entry at 50-70% then scale in only on confirmed strength. In an already-extended, high-ADX leader this low-volume pullback -- not the fresh breakout my own data shows fails at ADX>25 -- is where the fat pitch lives.

recent.topic: Correlation-adjusted position sizing: co-moving names are one bet (the effective-number-of-bets collapse), not many, and why that governs portfolio heat and the theme-risk cap
recent.summary: Diversification by COUNT is an illusion; only diversification by uncorrelated risk FACTORS reduces risk. For N equally-sized positions each with volatility sigma and pairwise correlation rho, portfolio volatility is sigma*sqrt([1+(N-1)*rho]/N): at rho=0 that is sigma/sqrt(N) (full benefit), but at rho->1 it goes to sigma, i.e. the N positions behave as ONE. The clean summary statistic is the effective number of independent bets, N_eff ~= N/[1+(N-1)*rho]; two names at rho~0.85 give N_eff~1.08 -- essentially a single bet. That is exactly my realized loss history: DELL and HPE were two tickers on ONE hyperscaler_server_capex driver, so a Meta-overbuild headline took both out at once, and my '2 positions' were 1 correlated bet the whole time. Attilio Meucci's Effective Number of Bets (exponential Shannon entropy of the diversification distribution) makes the same point formally: hidden correlation makes a book that LOOKS like N holdings act like ~1 exposure to one factor, and PCA can even hide this (minimum-torsion/factor framing is needed to see it). The Turtle system encoded the practitioner version as hard unit caps -- 4 units single market, 6 closely-correlated, 10 loosely, 12 in one direction -- precisely so a cluster of correlated trades could not become one oversized bet. Two cautions from the sources: (1) correlations RISE toward 1 in exactly the tail shock you are stopping for, so a benign-looking rho understates joint downside; (2) correlated stops fire and GAP together
recent.how_to_apply: Before any BUY, run the one-bet test using portfolio_risk and the demand_driver_map: if the candidate shares a holding's demand_driver OR shows corr_to_book > ~0.7, treat it as ADDING to an existing bet, not opening a new one -- size the pair against the THEME RISK <= 2% cap as a single position, never as two independent 1% risks (this is the DELL+HPE lesson made quantitative). When shared_left_tail is true, actively prefer a low/negative corr_to_book diversifier (diversifier=true) over a higher-conviction clone of what I already own, because at book level the clone adds almost no independent bet. Cite the actual number ('~0.85 correlated to DELL, N_eff ~1.1, so this is one hyperscaler_server_capex bet in two tickers'), not a vibe, and let the factor-stack cap / factor_response gate do its job rather than relabeling a name into a cheaper theme bucket. Because correlations rise and stops gap together in the exact shock I am stopped for, on a correlated add I size on realized (gap-adjusted) risk -- lean to ~1.3-1.5R of modelled slippage and toward the lower end of size -- rather than assuming the stop caps the loss. recent.topic: Stop distance vs. holding horizon: the √t noise band, and why entry location (not stop width) is the binding lever on multi-week swings
recent.summary: A stop has one job: fire on evidence the thesis broke, not on ordinary noise. Kaminski & Lo (SIFR RR 63, 2008; J. Financial Markets 18(C):234-254, 2014) prove that under a random walk, stop-loss rules ALWAYS decrease expected return; they only add value when returns exhibit momentum/positive serial correlation, generating what they call a 'stopping premium' proportional to return persistence (empirically 50-100bp/month during stop-out periods, US equities 1950-2004). So a stop placed inside the random-walk noise band is a pure expected-return tax. The quantitative half comes from volatility scaling: noise excursion grows with the SQUARE ROOT of time, so a stop sized off a one-day ATR is roughly √N too tight for an N-day hold (√45 ≈ 6.7). Danielsson & Zigrand (J. Banking & Finance 30(10):2701-2713, 2006) show the √t rule is only valid under iid normal returns and under jump diffusion 'leads to a systematic underestimation of risk, whereby the degree of underestimation worsens with the time horizon [and] the jump intensity' — so for equities with earnings inside the horizon, ATR×√N is a FLOOR on the noise band, not a ceiling. The decisive consequence: NO static entry stop inside a 15% cap can cover a 45-day noise band. This is not a reason to widen stops (the cap and the 2:1 RR floor forbid it) — it is the proof that stop width is not the free lever. Entry location is. The stop must only survive until the thesis STARTS working, which is why the Chandelier Exit (verified formula
recent.how_to_apply: Before any BUY, run the horizon-vs-noise test: compare my stop distance (%) against the name's daily ATR% × √(days until the nearest real catalyst) — NOT the full holding_horizon_days. If the stop is inside that band, the setup is asking a coin-flip to pay me: either move the entry down near the structural swing low so the same stop sits beyond the band, shorten the stated horizon to match what the stop can actually survive, or pass. Never widen the stop to fix this — the 15% cap and the 2:1 RR floor make wide stops fail geometry anyway, and stop_engineering's min_stop_distance_pct is a ONE-DAY floor that I must stop treating as horizon-adequate. Prefer setups where the catalyst is near and the entry is at support, since both shrink the noise the stop must clear; a 40-day thesis with no catalyst for three weeks needs ~4×ATR of room just to survive to its own event, which usually breaches the cap and is a pass. Even a correct exit can leave upside on the table — that is not always a mistake, but winners that keep running teach PARTIALS and trails: bank some, let the rest work while thesis invalidators are intact. left_on_table = price ran further after you sold a winner. good_lock_in = price faded after you sold — banking was right. stopped_then_recovered = loss exit then bounce (possible noise stop). hold_winners_playbook.when_left_on_table_repeats: Use sell_fraction (e.g. 0.4–0.6) to bank, trail rest with structure (raise stop under higher lows / 50-DMA) while invalidators clear.
hold_winners_playbook.when_why_is_catalyst: Leftover gains were news/event-driven after exit — before full exits, check earnings/catalyst calendar; prefer partials into known events.
hold_winners_playbook.when_why_is_technical: Leftover gains were trend continuation without a clear new catalyst — if structure + invalidators still clear, trail instead of full close.
hold_winners_playbook.when_good_lock_in_repeats: Full exits into strength then fade are fine — do not force trails when leadership is rolling over.
hold_winners_playbook.never: Never ignore stops or invalidators just to 'let it run' — that is hope. Running winners means planned partials, not deleting risk.

adopted_lessons.note: ADOPTED LESSONS from the weekly pipeline (improvement notes → durable text). Treat as standing process commitments until a later review supersedes them. hard_pending items need owner/code — do not invent validator changes yourself. Superseded lessons are omitted.

lessons.text: ** Two process gaps cost research time today. First, candlestick charts did not render this run — `data/charts/` was empty even though the gather log said "rendering candlestick charts..."; the chart step appears to depend on the same blocked live yfinance feed rather than falling back to the relay bundle the way the rest of the pipeline does, so I judged entry geometry on numeric indicators alone with no visual confirmation of the actual price bars. Second, the watchlist-trigger-alert logic flagged AMD as "price trigger reached" when the price was actually 3.9% away from my stated $555 level

** For non-focus scan names that surface as genuine top candidates (MU this run — #2 EPS revision, cheapest-in-group, strong-buy), the bundle gives me the numeric row but withholds the chart, filing texts, options-implied move, and deep fundamentals I need to actually underwrite an entry — so a legitimately compelling name gets defaulted to the watchlist partly for lack of data rather than lack of merit. The scanner should promote the top 1–2 non-focus setups (by swing_setup_score or upward-revision rank) into the focus set each run so they receive a chart + deep bundle, letting me deep-resear
Daily study session produced no machine-readable lesson - prompt/parse needs attention.

Daily study (technical_analysis): Stop distance vs. holding horizon: the √t noise band, and why entry location (not stop width) is the binding lever on multi-week swings - A stop has one job: fire on evidence the thesis broke, not on ordinary noise. Kaminski & Lo (SIFR RR 63, 2008; J. Financial Markets 18(C):234-254, 2014) prove that under a random walk, stop-loss rules

** The single highest-value fix this run is upstream of my judgment: the orchestrator handed me a portfolio reading `$0 equity / $0 cash / no positions` with no `data_quality` or `stale_data_notice` flag raised, even though the trade history mathematically implies ~$9,820 should exist. A cheap deterministic guard — "if broker equity is ~$0 but closed-trade math implies non-trivial cash, flag `broker_sync_suspect` and set `allows_new_buys: false` with a reason" — would prevent a future run from being invited to trade (this was even a trigger-driven run) against an account it cannot possibly fun

** The deterministic trigger check fired on AMD purely because the *price* touched the parsed $500 level, but my published `would_buy_at` was a compound condition — *post-event* confirmation plus a 50-DMA reclaim, explicitly excluding a pre-event dip. The result is a full event-driven run spun up for a setup that was never actually live, five days before its own catalyst. The trigger parser could be materially sharper if it also parsed an *event/date gate* from the trigger text (e.g. "after 7/22-23") and suppressed or down-weighted the alert until that date passes, rather than firing on the pr
